name: Umar Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the neighbourhood team for the Old Town, so most days I'm on a bike, not in a car. I start at eight with the overnight log, then I ride round the market, the bus station and the arches where people sleep rough. A lot of it is knowing names: the shop owner who's had his window put through twice, the guy under the railway bridge who's off his medication. Around midday I usually meet Nadia, an outreach worker from the Lantern day centre, and we go and see who's new on the street.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part you'd miss if it went?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The slow conversations. On response you're in and out in twenty minutes, but here I can spend a week getting someone into a hostel. The paperwork I wouldn't miss, though I've started using the force's approved writing assistant to tidy up my weekly briefing notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me, to be honest. I've got enough going on without a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I say now: the writing assistant is handy for briefings, but it doesn't know anyone on my beat. The work is people, and people still need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm in a decent spot. The job's steady, my rent's split with my mate Tomas, and I've got about four months saved. My only real gripe is that the neighbourhood team keeps getting raided to cover response shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on doing the beat, keep using the writing tool for the boring bits. I'd keep putting 200 a month away like I do now. Maybe ask my sergeant again about the mental health liaison course, because half my calls are really mental health calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. It's the world I already know, with a slightly better spell-checker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the team gets raided for response shifts. How often?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one week in four I get pulled into a car for response, because they're short. Then the people on my beat don't see me, and the trust slips a bit. Nadia notices it straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it bother you if nothing changed at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd rather the money went on keeping the neighbourhood team full than on another gadget. If AI stays a small thing, I'll just keep using AI for the small things.

say: The writing assistant helps with **briefings**, but it doesn't know anyone on my beat.
Policing the Old Town is **people work**, and people still need people.
think: I'm in a **decent spot**: steady job, shared rent and about four months saved.
My only real gripe is the team being **raided for response** shifts.
do: Keep riding the **Old Town beat** and using the writing tool for briefing notes.
Save about **200 a month**, as I already do.
Ask my sergeant again for the **mental health liaison** course.
feel: Pretty **calm**, since it's the world I know with a better spell-checker.
S0.quote: If AI stays a small thing, I'll just keep using AI for the small things.
fieldNote: His pay feels **secure** and costs are shared, so a quiet AI world leaves him calm.
Already uses the **approved writing tool** for low-stakes notes, which fits his steady style.
His concern is **staffing raids** on the neighbourhood team, not technology.

steps.text: Keep riding the Old Town bike beat and meeting Nadia at midday
Keep saving 200 a month from his police pay
Ask the sergeant again for a place on the mental health liaison course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels real. Half the stuff on that list is already creeping into the station.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm open to it if it gets officers out of the station and onto the street. I'd also say on the team chat that savings from software shouldn't become an excuse to shrink neighbourhood policing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the risk for me isn't the software, it's the budget people. If AI can map hotspots and write the reports, someone will argue you need fewer officers walking around knowing names. My job is the sort that looks like a luxury on a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good at the new tools once the first teams show they work, so I'm not the one dragging. I'd join the officers' association working group on AI, because neighbourhood officers need a voice in it. And I'd keep my savings going, maybe bump it to 250 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's probably safe, but the bit of policing I love is the bit that's easiest to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the cut actually look like on your beat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably they'd merge the Old Town team with the Riverside one, so four of us cover twice the streets. I'd see Nadia once a week instead of every day. The people under the arches would just see a camera on a pole instead of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the software. The people who decide budgets and see a cheaper option and take it, every time. Policing by camera saves money on paper and costs a lot more in trust.

say: I'm **open to AI** if it gets officers out of the station and onto the street.
Software savings shouldn't become an **excuse to shrink** neighbourhood policing.
think: The real risk is **budget holders** deciding fewer officers can walk the beat.
Neighbourhood work looks like a **luxury on a spreadsheet**, even though it isn't.
do: Learn the **new report tools** properly once the first teams show they work.
Join the officers' association **working group on AI** for neighbourhood officers.
Raise my savings to about **250 a month**.
feel: Uneasy that the **part I love** is the part easiest to cut.
S1.quote: The people under the arches would just see a camera on a pole instead of me.
fieldNote: Blames **budget decisions**, not technology, which fits his progressive outlook.
Expects a **team merger** rather than losing his own job, so uneasy rather than anxious.
Plans to learn tools once **proven**, matching his steady approach.

steps.text: Learn the force's new report and hotspot tools once other teams use them
Join the officers' association working group on AI in policing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking side, five for robots. That's not long at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say we need laws fast about what machines can do in policing, and I'd post that and sign whatever went round. I'd also say we shouldn't panic, because the street work doesn't go overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, by 2028 the reports, the intelligence work, maybe even the decisions about where to send officers go to AI. My beat is mostly hands-on and talking, so I've got until about 2031. But I'd be thirty in a job that's on the clock, and I don't know what I'd switch to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd push hard for the mental health liaison course, or pay for a mental health first aid certificate myself, about 300. I'd raise savings to 300 a month and stop the gym membership I barely use. And I'd write to my councillor about keeping human officers for anything involving vulnerable people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, because I've got some savings and a few years of street work, but it's on my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why mental health work, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's where machines would be worst. You can't send a robot to talk a man down off the multi-storey car park on Bridge Street. I did that last winter with Nadia, and it took ninety minutes of just talking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tomas, your flatmate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas drives the number 12 bus, and honestly I think his job goes before mine. I'd tell him we both need a plan, and maybe we stop talking about renting a bigger flat next year.

say: We need **laws fast** on what machines can do in policing.
Nobody should **panic**, because street work doesn't vanish overnight.
think: By **2028** reports and intelligence work go to AI, and my beat lasts until about 2031.
At thirty I'd be in a job **on the clock** with no clear switch.
do: Pay about **300** for a mental health first aid certificate if the force won't fund one.
Raise savings to **300 a month** and cancel the unused gym membership.
Write to my **councillor** about human officers for vulnerable people.
feel: **Anxious** but not panicking, thanks to some savings and a few years of street work.
S2.quote: You can't send a robot to talk a man down off the multi-storey car park on Bridge Street.
fieldNote: Clearly reads the **three-year gap**: desk work in 2028, his hands-on beat about 2031.
Mental health work is his chosen **safe ground**, rooted in a real rescue.
Worries his flatmate's **bus job** goes first, which shakes plans for a bigger flat.

steps.text: Pay for a mental health first aid certificate this spring
Cancel the gym membership and save 300 a month
Write to the councillor about human officers for vulnerable people
Drop the plan to rent a bigger flat with Tomas next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to get a plan going, if I don't sit on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for the force to train people up, not cut them. Five years is plenty of time to move officers into the roles machines won't do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel like I can see the road. By 2031 the paperwork's gone, around 2034 the patrolling is, and I'd be thirty-four with time to change. I'm not one to jump first, but once I see others doing it, I'll go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get on the mental health liaison course within the year and use the AI tools more on the desk side, so I know what they can and can't do. I'd keep saving the extra 50 a month. After a couple of years I'd look at a street triage post with the health service, where police and nurses go out together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than worried. There's time, and I can see where I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you think the triage post would last longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's half health, half police, and the health side is about sitting with someone in crisis. I'm not saying a machine can't help, but people don't open up to a tablet. At least that's my guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't jump first. What would make you jump?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing two or three people I know move into those roles and like it. My mate Leon from training went into a liaison post last year, and if Leon says the post is good, I'll trust that more than any leaflet.

say: This is the moment for the force to **train people up**, not cut them.
Five years is **plenty of time** to move officers into roles machines won't do well.
think: I can **see the road**: paperwork gone by 2031 and patrol around 2034.
I won't **jump first**, but once others go, I'll follow.
do: Get on the **mental health liaison** course within the year.
Use the force's **AI tools** more on the desk side to learn their limits.
Apply for a **street triage post** with the health service after a couple of years.
feel: Uneasy rather than worried, because there's **time** and a clear direction.
S3.quote: My mate Leon from training went into a liaison post last year, and if Leon says the post is good, I'll trust that more than any leaflet.
fieldNote: The extra years turn his fear into a **step-by-step** plan.
He'll move when **trusted peers** go first, which suits his steady style.
Believes **crisis work** needs a human presence but admits that's a guess.

steps.text: Complete the force's mental health liaison course within a year
Use the force's AI report tools to learn what they get wrong
Apply for a street triage post with the health service by 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking AI lands and about forty when the robots do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's use it to set fair rules and retrain people properly. I'd post that unions and government should start planning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fine. Ten years is time to get qualified and settled in a role that's mostly about people in crisis. I'd also still be young enough to start again at forty if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the beat for now, do the liaison course in the next year or two, and maybe study part-time for a mental health nursing qualification after that. I'd keep my savings ticking along at 200 a month. No big moves until I see where things are heading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's a long way off, and I'd be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave policing completely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if the nursing route opened up. I like the job, but I joined the police to help people on bad days, not to wear a uniform for its own sake. If a nursing badge does that better in 2036, I'd take the nursing badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Nadia about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Nadia that outreach is probably safer than my job, and that I might end up on her side of the street. She'd laugh and tell me the pay's worse.

say: We've got a **decade**, so let's set fair rules and retrain people properly.
Unions and government should **start planning** now, not later.
think: Ten years is time to get **qualified** in a role about people in crisis.
I'd still be young enough to **start again** at forty.
do: Keep the **Old Town beat** while doing the liaison course in a year or two.
Study part-time for a **mental health nursing** qualification afterwards.
Keep saving about **200 a month** and make no big moves yet.
feel: Mostly **calm**, because the change is far off and he'd be ready.
S4.quote: I joined the police to help people on bad days, not to wear a uniform for its own sake.
fieldNote: A **decade** makes him calm, as he has time to qualify in crisis work.
Shows real **openness** to leaving policing for nursing.
His identity rests on **helping people**, not on the uniform.

steps.text: Keep the Old Town neighbourhood beat for the next few years
Start a part-time mental health nursing qualification after the liaison course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because street work only buys me three years. What would help is the force paying for mental health training now and guaranteeing human officers for anyone vulnerable.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people on the street. When I'm moved off the beat, the people under the arches lose the one officer who knows their name.

headlineQuote: Policing by camera saves money on paper and costs a lot more in trust.
portrait: Umar is a **27-year-old** neighbourhood officer on a bike beat in the Old Town, sharing a flat with his friend Tomas.
He uses the force's **writing assistant** for small jobs and adopts tools once they're proven.
He blames **budget holders**, not machines, for the risk to neighbourhood policing.
He's calm in quiet worlds and **anxious** under fast AGI, with only three extra years of street work.
His plan everywhere points to **mental health** crisis work, maybe nursing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because street work only buys him about three years.
whatWouldHelp: The force **paying for** mental health training now.
A guarantee of **human officers** for anyone vulnerable.
